verses.text: Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle and set apart for God's Good News,
which God had promised long ago through his prophets in the holy Scriptures.
This Good News is about his Son, who in his human life was descended from David,
and who was shown with power to be God's Son by the Spirit of holiness through his resurrection from the dead: Jesus Christ our Lord.
Through him we received grace and the calling to be apostles, so that people among all nations would come to the obedience that faith brings, for the sake of his name.
And you are among them too, called to belong to Jesus Christ.
To everyone in Rome whom God loves and has called to be his holy people: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because people everywhere are talking about your faith.
God, whom I serve with my whole spirit in sharing the Good News about his Son, is my witness that I keep mentioning you in my prayers.
I ask that, if God wills, I may finally be able to visit you.
I really want to see you so I can share some spiritual gift that will help strengthen you,
or, more accurately, so that we can encourage one another through each other's faith, yours and mine.
Brothers and sisters, I don't want you to miss this: I've often planned to visit you, but have been held back until now. I want to see some fruit among you too, just as among the other Gentiles.
I owe this message to Greeks and to people from other cultures, to the educated and the uneducated alike.
So I'm eager to share the Good News with you in Rome too, as far as it depends on me.
I'm not ashamed of the Good News about Christ. It's God's power to save everyone who believes, first the Jew and also the Greek.
In it, God's righteousness is revealed through faith and leads to faith. As Scripture says, ‘The righteous will live by faith.’
God's anger is revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wrongdoing of people who use their wrongdoing to bury the truth.
What can be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them.
Ever since the world was created, God's invisible qualities—his eternal power and divine nature—have been clearly seen in what he made. So people have no excuse.
They knew God, but they didn't honor him as God or thank him. Instead, their thinking became empty, and their foolish hearts went dark.
They claimed to be wise, but became fools,
and traded the glory of the immortal God for images shaped like mortal humans, birds, animals, and reptiles.
So God let them follow the desires of their hearts into impurity, and they dishonored their own bodies among themselves.
They traded God's truth for a lie, and worshiped and served what was created instead of the Creator, who is praised forever. Amen.
Because of this, God let them follow degrading passions. Their women exchanged natural relations for those that go against nature.

In the same way, the men also left natural relations with women and burned with desire for one another. Men did shameful things with men and received in themselves the fitting consequence of their error.
Since they refused to keep God in their knowledge, God let them follow a corrupt way of thinking and do what should not be done.
They became full of every kind of wrongdoing: sexual sin, evil, greed, and malice. They were full of envy, murder, fighting, deceit, and spite; they gossiped,
slandered, hated God, acted arrogantly and abusively, bragged, dreamed up new ways to do evil, and disobeyed their parents.
They were foolish, unfaithful, heartless, and merciless.
They know God's ruling: people who practice these things deserve death. Yet they do them anyway—and even cheer on others who do the same.
So you have no excuse, whoever you are when you judge someone else. When you judge them, you condemn yourself, because you who judge do the same things.
We know God's judgment against people who do such things is based on the truth.
Do you really think you will escape God's judgment, even though you judge people who do these things while doing them yourself?
Or do you look down on God's rich kindness, restraint, and patience? Don't you see that God's kindness is meant to lead you to turn back to him?
But because your heart is stubborn and won't turn back, you're storing up judgment for yourself on the day when God's righteous judgment is revealed.
God ‘will repay each person according to what they have done.’
To those who keep doing good and seek glory, honor, and immortality, he will give eternal life.
But to those who are self-centered, reject the truth, and follow wrongdoing, there will be anger and fury.
There will be trouble and distress for every person who does evil—for the Jew first, and also for the Greek.
But glory, honor, and peace will come to everyone who does good—for the Jew first, and also for the Greek.
God doesn't play favorites.
Everyone who sinned without the law will perish without the law, and everyone who sinned under the law will be judged by the law.
It's not the people who hear the law who are right with God. The ones who do what the law says will be declared right.
(When Gentiles who don't have the law naturally do what the law requires, they become a law to themselves, even though they don't have the law.
They show that what the law requires is written on their hearts. Their conscience confirms it, and their thoughts sometimes accuse them and sometimes defend them.)
This will happen on the day God judges people's hidden lives through Jesus Christ, according to the Good News I proclaim.
Now, if you call yourself a Jew, rely on the law, and take pride in God,
if you know his will and can recognize what matters because you've been taught from the law,
if you're sure you can guide the blind and be a light for people in the dark,
correct the foolish, teach the young, and claim to have the pattern of knowledge and truth in the law—
then you who teach others, don't you teach yourself? You preach against stealing, but do you steal?
You say people must not commit adultery, but do you commit adultery? You hate idols, but do you rob temples?
You take pride in the law, but do you dishonor God by breaking it?
As Scripture says, ‘God's name is insulted among the Gentiles because of you.’
Circumcision is valuable if you obey the law. But if you break the law, your circumcision counts for nothing.
So if someone uncircumcised keeps the law's requirements, won't God count that person as circumcised?
Won't the one who is physically uncircumcised but obeys the law condemn you, who have the written law and circumcision but break the law?
A person isn't a Jew just because of outward appearance, and circumcision isn't only an outward mark on the body.
A Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, brought about by the Spirit, not by a written code. That person's praise comes from God, not people.
So what advantage does the Jew have? What good is circumcision?
A lot, in every way. First of all, they were entrusted with God's words.
What if some of them were unfaithful? Does that make God unfaithful too?
Absolutely not! Let God be true, even if every person is a liar. As Scripture says, ‘So you will be shown right in what you say and win when you are judged.’
But if our wrongdoing makes God's righteousness stand out, what should we say? Is God wrong to bring judgment? (I'm speaking from a human point of view.)
Absolutely not! Otherwise, how could God judge the world?
If my lie makes God's truth shine even brighter and brings him glory, why am I still judged as a sinner?
Why not say—as some falsely accuse us of saying—‘Let's do evil so good can come’? Those who say that deserve their condemnation.
So are we better off? Not at all. We've already charged that both Jews and Greeks are under sin.
As Scripture says: ‘No one is righteous—not even one.
No one understands; no one seeks God.
Everyone has turned away; together they have become useless. No one does good—not even one.’
‘Their throat is an open grave; their tongues tell lies.’ ‘Viper venom is under their lips.’
‘Their mouths are full of curses and bitter words.’
‘Their feet rush to spill blood.
Ruin and misery mark their paths.
They haven't known the way of peace.’
‘There is no fear of God before their eyes.’
We know that everything the law says is spoken to those under the law, so every mouth will be silenced and the whole world held accountable to God.
No one will be made right with God by doing what the law requires. The law shows us what sin is.
But now, apart from the law, God's righteousness has been revealed. The Law and the Prophets bear witness to it.
This righteousness from God comes through faith in Jesus Christ to everyone who believes. There is no difference,
because everyone has sinned and falls short of God's glory.
Yet God freely makes people right through his grace, by the rescue that is in Christ Jesus.
God presented Christ as the sacrifice that deals with sin through faith in his blood. This showed God's righteousness, because in his patience he had passed over sins committed earlier.
He did this to show his righteousness now, so he could be just and also make right the person who trusts in Jesus.
So where is there room to brag? It's shut out. By what principle—works? No, by the principle of faith.
We conclude that a person is made right through faith, apart from doing what the law commands.
Or is God only the God of Jews? Isn't he also the God of Gentiles? Yes, he is,
since there is one God, who makes the circumcised right by faith and the uncircumcised right through faith.
So does faith cancel the law? Absolutely not! It confirms the law.
So what can we say Abraham, our ancestor by human descent, gained?
If Abraham was made right by what he did, he could brag—but not before God.
What does Scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God, and God counted him as righteous.’
When someone works, their pay isn't a gift; it's what they're owed.
But when someone doesn't rely on their work and instead trusts God, who makes the ungodly right, that faith is counted as righteousness.
David says the same thing when he describes the blessing God gives apart from works:
‘Blessed are those whose lawless acts are forgiven and whose sins are covered.
Blessed is the person whose sin the Lord will never count against them.’
Is this blessing only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? We say Abraham's faith was counted as righteousness.
So when was it counted—after he was circumcised or before? Not after, but before.

He received circumcision as a sign and a seal of the righteousness that came through faith while he was still uncircumcised. This made him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so righteousness could be counted to them too.
He is also the father of the circumcised who don't just have the mark, but follow the footsteps of the faith our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.
The promise to Abraham and his descendants that he would inherit the world didn't come through the law. It came through righteousness by faith.
If the heirs were those who rely on the law, faith would be pointless and the promise would be canceled.
The law brings judgment. Where there is no law, there is no breaking of the law either.

That's why the promise comes by faith: so it can be a gift of grace and be guaranteed to all Abraham's descendants—not only those who have the law, but also those who share Abraham's faith. He is the father of us all.
As Scripture says, ‘I have made you the father of many nations.’ Abraham trusted God, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence what doesn't exist.
When hope seemed gone, Abraham still trusted in hope, believing he would become the father of many nations, just as God had said: ‘Your descendants will be so numerous.’
His faith didn't weaken, even though he knew his body was as good as dead—he was about a hundred years old—and Sarah's womb was unable to bear children.
He didn't let unbelief make him doubt God's promise. Instead, his faith grew stronger, and he gave glory to God.
He was fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.
That is why his faith ‘was counted to him as righteousness.’
Those words weren't written only for Abraham,
but also for us. God will count us righteous too when we believe in the one who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.
Jesus was handed over because of our trespasses and raised to make us right with God.
Since we've been made right through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Through him, by faith, we've entered this grace where we stand. And we celebrate the hope of sharing God's glory.
And there's more: we can even find joy in our troubles, because we know trouble builds endurance,
endurance shapes proven character, and proven character grows hope.
This hope won't let us down, because God has poured his love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit he gave us.
While we were still helpless, at just the right time Christ died for the ungodly.
Hardly anyone would die for a righteous person—though someone might dare to die for a truly good person.
But God shows his love for us this way: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
So now that we've been made right by his blood, we will be saved from God's anger through him all the more.
If we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son while we were enemies, how much more, now that we're reconciled, will we be saved through his life!
And that's not all—we celebrate in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we've now received reconciliation.
Sin entered the world through one man, and death came through sin. In this way death spread to everyone, because everyone sinned.
Sin was already in the world before the law was given, but sin isn't counted as breaking a law when there is no law.
Even so, death ruled from Adam to Moses, including over people whose sin wasn't like Adam's disobedience. Adam was a pattern pointing to the one who was to come.
But the gift isn't like the trespass. If many died because of one man's trespass, God's grace and the gift that came through the grace of one man, Jesus Christ, overflowed to many even more.
The gift isn't like the result of one man's sin. Judgment from one trespass brought condemnation, but the gift after many trespasses brings people into right standing with God.
If death ruled through that one man's trespass, how much more will those who receive overflowing grace and the gift of righteousness rule in life through the one man, Jesus Christ!
So then, one trespass brought condemnation for everyone; in the same way, one righteous act brings justification and life for everyone.
Just as one man's disobedience made many sinners, one man's obedience will make many righteous.
The law came in so trespasses would increase. But where sin increased, grace overflowed even more,
so that just as sin ruled through death, grace might rule through righteousness and bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
So what should we say? Should we keep sinning so grace can increase?
Absolutely not! We died to sin—how could we keep living in it?
Don't you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?
So through baptism we were buried with him into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the Father's glory, we too could live a new life.
If we've been united with him in a death like his, we'll also be united with him in a resurrection like his.
We know our old self was crucified with him so that sin's power over our bodies would be broken and we wouldn't be slaves to sin anymore.
Anyone who has died has been released from sin.
If we died with Christ, we believe we'll also live with him.
We know Christ was raised from the dead and won't die again. Death no longer rules over him.
The death he died, he died to sin once for all. The life he lives, he lives for God.
In the same way, count yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
So don't let sin rule your mortal body or make you obey its desires.

Don't hand over any part of yourselves to sin as a tool for wrongdoing. Instead, offer yourselves to God as people brought from death to life, and offer every part of yourselves to him as a tool for doing what is right.
Sin won't rule over you, because you're under grace, not under law.
So what then? Should we sin because we're under grace and not under law? Absolutely not!
Don't you know that when you offer yourselves to someone as obedient slaves, you're slaves of the one you obey—either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?
Thank God! You used to be slaves of sin, but you obeyed from the heart the teaching you were entrusted with.
You've been set free from sin and have become slaves of righteousness.

I'm putting this in everyday terms because of your human limitations. Just as you once handed yourselves over as slaves to impurity and ever-increasing wrongdoing, now offer yourselves as slaves to righteousness, which leads to holiness.
When you were slaves of sin, you weren't committed to righteousness.
What did you gain from the things you're now ashamed of? Those things end in death.
But now you've been set free from sin and become God's slaves. The result is a life set apart for God, and the outcome is eternal life.
Sin pays its wages in death, but God's free gift is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Brothers and sisters, since I'm speaking to people who know the law, don't you know that the law has authority over someone only as long as they live?
A married woman is bound by law to her husband while he is alive. But if he dies, she is released from the law concerning her husband.
So if she marries another man while her husband is alive, she's called an adulteress. But if her husband dies, she's free from that law, and marrying another man doesn't make her an adulteress.
In the same way, my brothers and sisters, you died to the law through Christ's body so you could belong to another—to Christ, who was raised from the dead—so that we could bear fruit for God.
When we lived by our human nature, sinful desires stirred up by the law were at work in us, producing fruit that led to death.
But now we've been released from the law, having died to what held us captive, so we can serve in the new way of the Spirit, not the old way of the written code.

So what should we say? Is the law sinful? Absolutely not! I wouldn't have known what sin was except through the law. I wouldn't have known what it means to covet if the law hadn't said, ‘You must not covet.’
But sin seized the opportunity the commandment gave it and stirred up every kind of coveting in me. Without the law, sin is dead.
There was a time when I was alive apart from the law. But when the commandment came, sin sprang to life, and I died.
The commandment that was meant to lead to life turned out to bring death to me.
Sin used the commandment to trick me and, through it, kill me.
So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, right, and good.
So did something good bring death to me? Absolutely not! Sin did, using what is good to produce death in me, so sin would be exposed as sin and shown to be utterly sinful through the commandment.
We know the law is spiritual, but I am human, sold as a slave to sin.
I don't understand what I'm doing. I don't do what I want to do; instead, I do what I hate.
And if I do what I don't want to do, I agree that the law is good.
So it's no longer I who do it, but sin living in me.
I know that nothing good lives in me—that is, in my human nature. I want to do what is good, but I can't carry it out.
I don't do the good I want to do. Instead, I keep doing the evil I don't want to do.
So if I do what I don't want to do, it's no longer I doing it, but sin living in me.
Here's the pattern I find: I want to do what is good, but evil is right there with me.
Deep down, I delight in God's law,
but I see another law at work in my body, fighting against the law in my mind and making me a prisoner of the law of sin at work in me.
What a miserable person I am! Who will rescue me from this body headed for death?
Thank God—he rescues me through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, in my mind I serve God's law, but in my human nature I serve sin's law.
So there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who live by the Spirit instead of by their human nature.
The Spirit's law of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death.
The law couldn't free us because our human nature made it powerless. So God did: he sent his own Son in a human life like ours, to deal with sin, and condemned sin in that human life.
He did this so the law's just requirement could be fulfilled in us, as we live by the Spirit and not by our human nature.
Those who live by their human nature focus on what that nature wants. Those who live by the Spirit focus on what the Spirit wants.
A mind set on human nature leads to death, but a mind set on the Spirit brings life and peace.
A mind set on human nature is hostile to God. It doesn't submit to God's law—in fact, it can't.
Those who live by their human nature can't please God.
But you aren't living by your human nature; you're living by the Spirit, if God's Spirit truly lives in you. Anyone who doesn't have the Spirit of Christ doesn't belong to him.
If Christ is in you, your body is subject to death because of sin, but the Spirit is life because of righteousness.
If the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus from the dead lives in you, the one who raised Christ Jesus will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit living in you.
So then, brothers and sisters, we owe nothing to our human nature that would make us live by it.
If you live by your human nature, you'll die. But if by the Spirit you put the body's deeds to death, you'll live.
All who are led by God's Spirit are God's children.
You didn't receive a spirit of slavery that pulls you back into fear. You received the Spirit who makes you God's adopted children, and by him we cry, ‘Abba, Father!’
The Spirit himself confirms to our spirit that we are God's children.
And if we're children, we're heirs too—heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, if we share his suffering so we can also share his glory.
I consider that what we suffer now can't compare with the glory that will soon be revealed to us.
All creation waits with eager expectation for God's children to be revealed.
Creation was made subject to frustration, not by its own choice but by the one who subjected it, in the hope
that creation itself will be set free from slavery to decay and share in the glorious freedom of God's children.
We know that all creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth right up to now.
And not only creation—we who have the first taste of the Spirit groan inwardly too as we wait for God to adopt us fully and redeem our bodies.
We were saved in this hope. But if we can already see what we hope for, that's not hope—who hopes for what they already see?
But if we hope for what we don't see, we wait for it with patience.
In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. We don't know what we should pray for, but the Spirit himself pleads for us with groans too deep for words.
The one who searches our hearts knows what the Spirit intends, because the Spirit pleads for God's people in line with God's will.
We know that God works all things together for good for those who love him and are called according to his purpose.
Those he knew beforehand, he also chose beforehand to be shaped into the likeness of his Son, so that the Son would be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters.
Those he chose beforehand, he also called; those he called, he also made right; and those he made right, he also glorified.
So what can we say about all this? If God is for us, who can stand against us?
God didn't spare his own Son but gave him up for us all. Won't he also, along with him, freely give us everything we need?
Who can bring a charge against God's chosen people? God is the one who makes them right.
Who can condemn us? Christ Jesus is the one who died—and more than that, who was raised. He's at God's right hand, and he's also pleading for us.
Who can separate us from Christ's love? Trouble, hardship, persecution, hunger, poverty, danger, or violence?
As Scripture says, ‘For your sake we're being killed all day long; we're treated like sheep headed for slaughter.’
No! In all these things we have complete victory through the one who loved us.
I'm convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor rulers, neither what is happening now nor what is coming, nor any powers,
neither height nor depth nor anything else in all creation can separate us from God's love in Christ Jesus our Lord.
I tell the truth in Christ—I'm not lying. My conscience confirms it through the Holy Spirit:
I carry deep sorrow and unending pain in my heart.
I could wish that I myself were cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers and sisters, my own people by human descent.
They are Israelites. Theirs are adoption, glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, worship, and the promises.
The patriarchs belong to them, and from them, in his human ancestry, came the Messiah, who is God over all, praised forever. Amen.
But God's word hasn't failed. Not everyone descended from Israel truly belongs to Israel.
And not all of Abraham's descendants are his children. Rather, Scripture says, ‘Your descendants will be traced through Isaac.’
That means physical descendants aren't automatically God's children. The children of the promise are counted as Abraham's offspring.
For this is the promise: ‘At the appointed time I will return, and Sarah will have a son.’
And that's not all. Rebekah also became pregnant by one man, our father Isaac.
Before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, God's purpose in choosing could stand—not because of works, but because of the one who calls.
Rebekah was told, ‘The older will serve the younger.’
As Scripture also says, ‘I loved Jacob, but I rejected Esau.’
So what should we say? Is God unjust? Absolutely not!
God told Moses, ‘I will show mercy to whomever I choose to show mercy, and compassion to whomever I choose to show compassion.’
So it doesn't depend on what someone wants or tries to do, but on God, who shows mercy.
Scripture says to Pharaoh, ‘I raised you up for this very purpose: to show my power through you and make my name known throughout the earth.’
So God shows mercy to whom he chooses, and he hardens whom he chooses.
You might ask me, ‘Then why does God still blame people? Who can resist what he wants?’
But who are you, a human being, to argue back to God? Can what was made say to its maker, ‘Why did you make me like this?’
Doesn't a potter have the right to make from the same lump of clay one pot for honored use and another for ordinary use?
What if God, wanting to show his anger and make his power known, patiently endured objects of anger prepared for destruction?
And what if he did this to make the riches of his glory known to objects of mercy, which he prepared in advance for glory—
including us, whom he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles?
As God says in Hosea: ‘I will call those who were not my people my people, and the one who was not loved my beloved.’
‘And where they were told, You are not my people, they will be called children of the living God.’
Isaiah cries out about Israel: ‘Even if the number of Israel's children is like the sand of the sea, only a remnant will be saved.
For the Lord will carry out his word on earth, completely and without delay.’
And as Isaiah said earlier, ‘If the Lord of Armies hadn't left us descendants, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.’
So what should we say? Gentiles who weren't pursuing righteousness received it—the righteousness that comes through faith.
But Israel, pursuing a law meant to bring righteousness, didn't reach that goal.
Why? Because they pursued it as if it came from works instead of faith. They stumbled over the stumbling stone,
just as Scripture says: ‘Look, I am placing in Zion a stone that makes people stumble, a rock that trips them up; but whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.’
Brothers and sisters, what I want most, and what I pray to God for, is that Israel would be saved.
I can testify about them: they have a real passion for God, but it isn't guided by understanding.
They don't understand God's way of making people right. Trying to establish their own, they haven't submitted to God's righteousness.
Christ is the goal of the law, so that everyone who believes can be made right with God.
Moses writes about righteousness through the law: ‘The person who does these things will live by them.’
But righteousness through faith says: ‘Don't say in your heart, Who will go up to heaven?’ (That would be to bring Christ down.)
‘Or ask, Who will go down into the abyss?’ (That would be to bring Christ up from the dead.)
But what does it say? ‘The message is near you—in your mouth and in your heart.’ That's the message of faith we're preaching:
If you declare with your mouth, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
With the heart a person believes and is made right with God; with the mouth a person declares faith and is saved.
Scripture says, ‘Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.’
There is no difference between Jew and Greek. The same Lord is Lord of everyone and richly blesses all who call on him.
For Scripture says, ‘Everyone who calls on the Lord's name will be saved.’
But how can people call on someone they haven't believed in? How can they believe in someone they haven't heard about? And how can they hear without someone preaching to them?
And how can anyone preach unless they are sent? As Scripture says, ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who bring the Good News!’
But not everyone welcomed the Good News. Isaiah says, ‘Lord, who believed what we announced?’
So faith comes from hearing the message, and the message is heard through the word about Christ.
But I ask: Didn't they hear? Of course they did: ‘Their voice has gone out through all the earth, their words to the ends of the world.’
But I ask: Didn't Israel understand? First, Moses says, ‘I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; I will make you angry through a people without understanding.’
Then Isaiah speaks boldly: ‘I was found by those who weren't looking for me. I showed myself to those who weren't asking for me.’
But about Israel he says, ‘All day long I held out my hands to a disobedient and stubborn people.’
So I ask: Has God rejected his people? Absolutely not! I'm an Israelite myself, a descendant of Abraham from the tribe of Benjamin.
God has not rejected his people, whom he knew beforehand. Don't you remember what Scripture says about Elijah, when he appealed to God against Israel?
He said, ‘Lord, they've killed your prophets and torn down your altars. I'm the only one left, and now they're trying to kill me too.’
But what did God tell him? ‘I've kept seven thousand for myself who have never bowed to Baal.’
It's the same now: a remnant has been chosen by grace.
And if it's by grace, it's no longer based on works; otherwise grace wouldn't be grace. If it's based on works, then it's no longer grace; otherwise work wouldn't be work.
So what happened? Israel didn't get what it was seeking. The chosen ones received it, while the rest were hardened,
as Scripture says: ‘God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that can't see and ears that can't hear, to this very day.’
David says: ‘May their table become a trap and a snare, a stumbling block and a fitting punishment.
May their eyes grow dark so they can't see, and may their backs stay bent forever.’
So I ask: Did they stumble in order to fall beyond recovery? Absolutely not! Their trespass brought salvation to the Gentiles, to make Israel jealous.
If their trespass brought riches to the world, and their loss brought riches to the Gentiles, how much greater will their full inclusion be!
I'm speaking to you Gentiles. Since I'm an apostle to the Gentiles, I take pride in my ministry,
hoping somehow to make my own people jealous and save some of them.
If their rejection brought the world's reconciliation, what will their acceptance be? Life from the dead!
If the first part of the dough is offered as holy, then the whole batch is holy. If the root is holy, so are the branches.
If some branches were broken off, and you—a wild olive branch—were grafted in among them and now share the rich root of the olive tree,
don't brag over the branches. If you do, remember: you don't support the root; the root supports you.
You may say, ‘Branches were broken off so I could be grafted in.’
That's true. They were broken off because of unbelief, and you stand through faith. Don't get proud; stay humble.
If God didn't spare the natural branches, he won't spare you either.
So look at both God's kindness and his severity: severity toward those who fell, but kindness toward you—if you continue in his kindness. Otherwise, you'll be cut off too.
And if they don't remain in unbelief, they will be grafted in, because God can graft them in again.

If you were cut from a wild olive tree by nature and grafted, against nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more readily will these natural branches be grafted back into their own olive tree!
Brothers and sisters, I don't want you to miss this mystery and become conceited: a partial hardening has come over Israel until the full number of Gentiles comes in.
And in this way all Israel will be saved, as Scripture says: ‘The Deliverer will come from Zion; he will turn godlessness away from Jacob.
And this is my covenant with them when I take away their sins.’
As far as the Good News is concerned, they are enemies for your sake. But as far as God's choice is concerned, they are loved because of the patriarchs.
God's gifts and his call can't be taken back.
Just as you once disobeyed God but now received mercy because of their disobedience,
so they too have now disobeyed, in order that through the mercy shown to you they may also receive mercy.
For God has allowed everyone to be held in disobedience so he can show mercy to everyone.
How deep are God's riches, wisdom, and knowledge! His judgments are beyond searching out, and his ways are beyond tracing.
‘Who has known the Lord's mind? Who has ever been his adviser?’
‘Who has ever given God anything first, so that God should have to repay them?’
Everything comes from him, exists through him, and is for him. Glory to him forever! Amen.
So, brothers and sisters, because of God's mercy, I urge you to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice—holy and pleasing to God. This is your true and proper worship.
Don't let this age shape you. Instead, be transformed by a renewed mind, so you can recognize what God wants—what is good, pleasing, and complete.
By the grace given to me, I tell everyone among you: don't think of yourself more highly than you should. Think clearly and soberly, as God has given each person a measure of faith.
Just as one body has many parts, and those parts don't all have the same job,
so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and each of us belongs to one another.
We have different gifts according to the grace God has given us. If your gift is prophecy, use it in keeping with your faith.
If it's serving, then serve; if it's teaching, then teach.
If it's encouraging, then encourage; if it's giving, give generously; if it's leading, lead diligently; if it's showing mercy, do it cheerfully.
Let your love be real. Hate what is evil; hold tightly to what is good.
Love each other like family. Take the lead in showing honor to one another.
Don't lose your drive. Stay spiritually fired up as you serve the Lord.
Be joyful in hope, patient in trouble, and faithful in prayer.
Share with God's people who are in need. Make hospitality a habit.
Bless those who persecute you—bless them, don't curse them.
Celebrate with those who celebrate; mourn with those who mourn.
Live in harmony with one another. Don't chase status; be willing to spend time with people others overlook. Don't act like you know it all.
Don't pay anyone back with evil. Do what everyone can see is good.
If possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone.
Dear friends, don't take revenge. Leave room for God's anger, because Scripture says, ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord.’
Instead, ‘If your enemy is hungry, feed them; if they're thirsty, give them something to drink. By doing this, you'll heap burning coals on their head.’
Don't let evil defeat you. Defeat evil by doing good.
Everyone should submit to the governing authorities. No authority exists except by God's permission, and the authorities that do exist have been established by God.
So whoever resists authority is resisting what God has established, and those who resist will bring judgment on themselves.
Rulers aren't a threat to people who do good, but to those who do evil. Do you want to have no fear of the authorities? Do what's good, and they'll commend you,

because the ruler is God's servant for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid: the ruler doesn't carry the sword for nothing. They serve God as an agent of justice, bringing judgment on the wrongdoer.
So you should submit, not only to avoid punishment but also for the sake of your conscience.
That's also why you pay taxes: the authorities are God's servants, continually carrying out their duties.
Give everyone what you owe them: taxes to the tax collector, customs duties where they're owed, respect to those due respect, and honor to those due honor.
Don't owe anyone anything, except the debt of loving one another. Whoever loves their neighbor has fulfilled the law.
The commands—don't commit adultery, don't murder, don't steal, don't covet—and any other command are summed up in this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’
Love doesn't harm a neighbor. So love fulfills the law.
Do this because you know what time it is: it's time to wake up. Our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed.
The night is almost over, and the day is close. So let's throw off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light.
Let's live honorably, as people do in the daylight—not in wild parties and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and reckless behavior, and not in fighting and jealousy.
Instead, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and don't make plans to satisfy your human nature and its desires.
Welcome those whose faith is weak, but don't get into arguments over disputed opinions.
One person believes they can eat anything, while another, whose faith is weak, eats only vegetables.
The one who eats must not look down on the one who doesn't, and the one who doesn't eat must not judge the one who does. God has welcomed them.
Who are you to judge someone else's servant? Their own master decides whether they stand or fall. And they will stand, because the Lord is able to make them stand.
One person considers one day more special than another; someone else considers every day alike. Each should be fully convinced in their own mind.
Whoever observes a special day does so for the Lord. Whoever eats does so for the Lord, since they give thanks to God; whoever abstains does so for the Lord and gives thanks to God.
None of us lives for ourselves alone, and none of us dies for ourselves alone.
If we live, we live for the Lord; if we die, we die for the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.
This is why Christ died, came back to life, and lives again: to be Lord of both the dead and the living.
So why do you judge your brother or sister? And why do you look down on them? We will all stand before God's judgment seat.
For Scripture says, ‘As surely as I live, says the Lord, every knee will bow to me, and every tongue will praise God.’
So each of us will give an account of ourselves to God.
Let's stop judging one another. Instead, decide not to put an obstacle or trap in the way of a brother or sister.
I know, and am convinced in the Lord Jesus, that nothing is unclean by itself. But if someone considers something unclean, then for that person it is unclean.
If your brother or sister is hurt because of what you eat, you're no longer acting in love. Don't destroy someone Christ died for just because of your food.
So don't let what you consider good be spoken of as evil.
God's Kingdom isn't about food and drink. It's about righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.
Anyone who serves Christ this way is pleasing to God and respected by people.
So let's pursue what makes for peace and builds one another up.
Don't tear down God's work for the sake of food. Everything is clean, but it's wrong to eat in a way that trips someone up.
It's good not to eat meat, drink wine, or do anything that causes your brother or sister to stumble.
Whatever you believe about these things, keep it between yourself and God. Blessed is the person who doesn't condemn themselves by doing what they believe is right.
But whoever has doubts is condemned if they eat, because they aren't acting from faith. Anything that doesn't come from faith is sin.
Now to the one who can strengthen you according to my Good News and the message about Jesus Christ—the revelation of the mystery kept secret for long ages,
but now revealed and made known through the prophetic Scriptures, by the command of the eternal God, so that all nations may come to the obedience of faith—
to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, be glory forever! Amen.
Those of us who are strong ought to carry the weaknesses of those who aren't, instead of looking out only for ourselves.
Each of us should look out for our neighbor's good and build them up.
Even Christ didn't live to please himself. As Scripture says, ‘The insults aimed at you fell on me.’
Everything written long ago was written to teach us, so that through endurance and the encouragement of Scripture we could have hope.
May the God who gives endurance and encouragement help you live in harmony with one another, following Christ Jesus,
so that together, with one voice, you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
So welcome one another, just as Christ welcomed you, to God's glory.
I mean that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God's truthfulness by confirming the promises made to the patriarchs,
and so that the Gentiles would glorify God for his mercy. As Scripture says, ‘I will praise you among the Gentiles and sing to your name.’
Again it says, ‘Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people.’
And again, ‘Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles; let all peoples praise him.’
Isaiah also says, ‘The root of Jesse will come, one who rises to rule the nations; the Gentiles will put their hope in him.’
May the God of hope fill you with every kind of joy and peace as you trust him, so that by the Holy Spirit's power your hope will overflow.
My brothers and sisters, I'm convinced that you're full of goodness, filled with knowledge, and able to guide one another.
Still, I've written to you quite boldly in places to refresh your memory, because of the grace God gave me
to serve Christ Jesus among the Gentiles. I serve like a priest with God's Good News, so that the Gentiles may become an offering acceptable to God, made holy by the Holy Spirit.
So I have reason to take pride in my service to God through Christ Jesus.
I won't claim anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obey God, by what I've said and done,
through powerful signs and wonders, by the power of God's Spirit. From Jerusalem all the way to Illyricum, I've fully proclaimed the Good News about Christ.
My goal has been to share the Good News where Christ wasn't already known, so I wouldn't build on someone else's foundation.
As Scripture says, ‘Those who were never told about him will see, and those who haven't heard will understand.’
That's why I've been kept from coming to you so many times.
But now I have no more place to work in these regions, and for many years I've wanted to visit you.
I hope to see you when I travel to Spain and be helped on my way there by you—after I've enjoyed your company for a while.
But for now I'm going to Jerusalem to serve God's people there.
The believers in Macedonia and Achaia were glad to take up a contribution for the poor among God's people in Jerusalem.
They were glad to do it, and they do owe them something. Since the Gentiles shared in the Jews' spiritual blessings, they should serve them with material blessings too.
Once I've delivered this gift and made sure they receive it, I'll travel to Spain by way of your city.
I know that when I come to you, I'll come with the full blessing of Christ's Good News.
Brothers and sisters, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit's love, I urge you to join me in praying to God for me.
Pray that I'll be rescued from the disobedient in Judea and that my service in Jerusalem will be welcomed by God's people there.
Then, if God wills, I can come to you with joy and find rest with you.
May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.
I recommend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchreae. 🤝
Welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of God’s people. Help her with whatever she needs from you, because she has helped many people—including me. 💛
Give my greetings to Prisca and Aquila, my coworkers in Christ Jesus. 👋
They put their own lives on the line for me. I am thankful to them, and so are all the Gentile churches. 🙏
Greet the church that meets in their home. Also greet my dear Epaenetus, the first person in Achaia to belong to Christ. 🏠
Greet Mary, who worked so hard for you all. 💪
Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and fellow prisoners. They are well respected among the apostles and came to Christ before I did. ⛓️
Greet my dear friend Amplias in the Lord. 💛
Greet Urbanus, our coworker in Christ, and my dear Stachys. 👋
Greet Apelles, who has stood the test in Christ. Greet everyone in the household of Aristobulus. 🏠
Greet my relative Herodion. Greet those in the household of Narcissus who belong to the Lord. 🤝
Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who work hard in the Lord. Greet my dear Persis, who has worked so hard in the Lord. 💪
Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who has also been like a mother to me. 💛
Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and all the believers with them. 👋
Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, Olympas, and all God’s people with them. 🤝
Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ send you their greetings. 💋
Brothers and sisters, keep an eye out for people who cause divisions and trip others up, going against the teaching you received. Stay away from them. ⚠️
People like that do not serve our Lord Christ. They serve their own appetites, and with smooth talk and flattery they trick innocent people. 🎭
Your obedience is known everywhere, and I am glad about that. Keep your heads clear about what is good and stay innocent about what is evil. 🌱
The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. May the grace of our Lord Jesus be with you. ✨
Timothy, my coworker, sends you greetings. So do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my relatives. 👋
I, Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord. ✍️
Gaius, who hosts me and the whole church, sends you greetings. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus send their greetings too. 🏠
May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen! 🙌
